25|BACKGROUND
26|Abiraterone acetate plus prednisolone improves survival in men with relapsed pros-
27|tate cancer. We assessed the effect of this combination in men starting long-term
28|androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT), using a multigroup, multistage trial design.
29|METHODS
30|We randomly assigned patients in a 1:1 ratio to receive ADT alone or ADT plus abir
31|aterone acetate (1000 mg daily) and prednisolone (5 mg daily) (combination therapy).
32|Local radiotherapy was mandated for patients with node-negative, nonmetastatic
33|disease and encouraged for those with positive nodes. For patients with nonmeta-
34|static disease with no radiotherapy planned and for patients with metastatic disease,
35|treatment continued until radiologic, clinical, or prostate-specific antigen (PSA) pro-
36|gression; otherwise, treatment was to continue for 2 years or until any type of progres-
37|sion, whichever came first. The primary outcome measure was overall survival. The
38|intermediate primary outcome was failure-free survival (treatment failure was de-
39|fined as radiologic, clinical, or PSA progression or death from prostate cancer).
40|RESULTS
41|A total of 1917 patients underwent randomization from November 2011 through
42|January 2014. The median age was 67 years, and the median PSA level was 53 ng per
43|milliliter. A total of 52% of the patients had metastatic disease, 20% had node-positive
44|or node-indeterminate nonmetastatic disease, and 28% had node-negative, nonmeta-
45|static disease; 95% had newly diagnosed disease. The median follow-up was 40
46|months. There were 184 deaths in the combination group as compared with 262 in
47|the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.76;
48|P<0.001); the hazard ratio was 0.75 in patients with nonmetastatic disease and 0.61
49|in those with metastatic disease. There were 248 treatment-failure events in the
50|combination group as compared with 535 in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio,
51|0.29; 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.34; P<0.001); the hazard ratio was 0.21 in patients with non-
52|metastatic disease and 0.31 in those with metastatic disease. Grade 3 to 5 adverse
53|events occurred in 47% of the patients in the combination group (with nine grade 5
54|events) and in 33% of the patients in the ADT-alone group (with three grade 5 events).
55|CONCLUSIONS
56|Among men with locally advanced or metastatic prostate cancer, ADT plus abiraterone
57|and prednisolone was associated with significantly higher rates of overall and
58|failure-free survival than ADT alone. (Funded by Cancer Research U.K. and others;
59|STAMPEDE ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00268476, and Current Controlled Trials
60|number, ISRCTN78818544.)

3|Abiraterone for Prostate Cancer
4|T
5|he Systemic Therapy in Advancing
6|or Metastatic Prostate Cancer: Evaluation
7|of Drug Efficacy (STAMPEDE) trial recruits
8|patients commencing long-term androgen-depri-
9|vation therapy (ADT; orchiectomy or gonadotropin-
10|releasing hormone [GnRH] agonists or antago-
11|nists) for the first time for locally advanced or
12|metastatic prostate cancer. Several agents have
13|improved overall survival (docetaxel, abiraterone
14|acetate, enzalutamide, cabazitaxel, radium-223,
15|and sipuleucel-T)1-8 or reduced morbidity (zole-
16|dronic acid and denosumab)9-11 among such pa-
17|tients. These agents were initially investigated in
18|men with very advanced disease whose tumors
19|had progressed during first-line ADT, a disease
20|state now termed castration-resistant prostate
21|cancer.
22|The STAMPEDE trial uses a novel multigroup,
23|multistage (also called multiarm, multistage
24|[MAMS]) platform design12-14 to test whether the
25|addition of further treatments to ADT improves
26|overall survival if used in the first-line setting. It
27|uses intermediate activity analyses, based on
28|failure-free survival, to cease randomization to
29|research groups that are insufficiently active.12-14
30|We have previously reported that treatment with
31|docetaxel at the inception of ADT increased me-
32|dian survival from 71 months to 81 months as
33|well as overall survival (hazard ratio for death,
34|0.76).15,16 These results, along with those of a
35|systematic review that included other trials17-19
36|and of a meta-analysis,16 led to docetaxel becom-
37|ing a part of the standard of care for suitable
38|patients with prostate cancer who had not re-
39|ceived previous hormone therapy.
40|An important mechanism for escape from
41|tumor control by androgen ablation includes the
42|intracellular conversion of steroid precursors to
43|androgenic steroids by prostate-cancer cells.
44|Abiraterone acetate is a selective, irreversible in-
45|hibitor of CYP17, an enzyme that is critical in the
46|production of androgens in the testes, adrenal
47|glands, and prostate-tumor tissue. Inhibition of
48|CYP17 in combination with ADT results in a
49|more effective androgen depletion than can be
50|induced by surgical castration or by GnRH ana-
51|logues alone.20 Two large, phase 3 trials showed
52|that the addition of abiraterone acetate with pred-
53|nisolone to standard-of-care therapy prolonged
54|survival among men with castration-resistant
55|prostate cancer.4,5,21 The STAMPEDE trial is inves-
56|tigating whether the earlier use of abiraterone in
57|men who are initiating long-term ADT could
58|improve survival.
59|Methods
60|Trial Design and Patients
61|We used a multigroup, multistage platform de-
62|sign, incorporating a seamless phase 2-3 com-
63|ponent. The primary outcome was overall sur-
64|vival, defined as the time from randomization to
65|death from any cause. The intermediate primary
66|outcome was failure-free survival, defined as the
67|time to the first of the following forms of treat-
68|ment failure: biochemical (prostate-specific anti-
69|gen [PSA]) failure (see the protocol, available
70|with the full text of this article at NEJM.org);
71|progression of local, lymph-node, or distant
72|metastases; or death from prostate cancer. Second
73|ary outcome measures included adverse events,
74|symptomatic skeletal events, progression-free
75|survival (i.e., failure-free survival excluding bio-
76|chemical failure), prostate cancer-specific sur-
77|vival, and (data not shown) quality of life.
78|The rationale and design were described pre-
79|viously.12-14,22 Full details are provided in the pro-
80|tocol. In summary, eligible patients had prostate
81|cancer that was newly diagnosed and metastatic,
82|node-positive, or high-risk locally advanced (with
83|at least two of following: a tumor stage of T3 or
84|T4, a Gleason score of 8 to 10, and a PSA level
85|≥40 ng per milliliter) or disease that was previ-
86|ously treated with radical surgery or radiother
87|apy and was now relapsing with high-risk fea-
88|tures (in men no longer receiving therapy, a PSA
89|level >4 ng per milliliter with a doubling time of
90|<6 months, a PSA level >20 ng per milliliter,
91|nodal or metastatic relapse, or <12 months of
92|total ADT with an interval of >12 months with-
93|out treatment). Patients were intended for treat-
94|ment with long-term ADT that started no longer
95|than 12 weeks before randomization. There were
96|no age restrictions. Patients with clinically sig-
97|nificant cardiovascular disease (e.g., severe angi-
98|na, recent myocardial infarction, or a history of
99|cardiac failure) were excluded.
100|Trial Oversight and Conduct
101|The trial was sponsored by the U.K. Medical
102|Research Council (MRC) and conducted by the
103|MRC Clinical Trials Unit at University College

9|the design for this comparison (ADT plus abira
10|terone and prednisolone vs. ADT alone) and
11|participated in discussions on the progress of
12|the trial. Janssen also provided grant funding,
13|abiraterone acetate, and funds for drug distribu-
14|tion. Representatives from Janssen were invited
15|to comment on the manuscript. Further funding
16|for the platform was provided by Astellas Pharma,
17|Clovis Oncology, Novartis, Pfizer, and Sanofi
18|Aventis. The trial was conducted in accordance
19|with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
20|guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki, and
21|the appropriate regulatory and ethics approvals
22|were obtained. All the patients provided written
23|informed consent.
24|The analyses were driven by prespecified cri-
25|teria, and the decision to submit the manuscript
26|for publication was made by the members of the
27|Trial Management Group. Three authors at the
28|MRC Clinical Trials Unit at UCL accessed the raw
29|data; processed data that were released by the
30|independent data monitoring committee and trial
31|steering committee were available to all the co-
32|authors. The authors vouch for the completeness
33|and accuracy of the data and analyses and for the
34|adherence of the trial to the protocol. No one
35|who is not an author contributed to the writing
36|of the manuscript.
37|Randomization and Masking
38|Randomization was performed centrally by tele-
39|phone with the use of a computerized algorithm,
40|which was developed and maintained by the MRC
41|Clinical Trials Unit at UCL. Minimization with a
42|random element of 80% was used, with stratifi-
43|cation according to randomizing center, age at
44|randomization (<70 vs. ≥70 years), the presence
45|or absence of metastases, planned use of pros-
46|tate radiotherapy (yes vs. no), nodal involvement
47|(negative vs. indeterminate vs. positive), World
48|Health Organization performance status (0 vs.
49|1 or 2 [on a scale of 0 to 4, with higher numbers
50|indicating greater disability]), type of ADT, and
51|regular, long-term use of aspirin or nonsteroidal
52|antiinflammatory drugs (yes vs. no). The assign-
53|ment ratio was 1:1 to standard of care alone or
54|with abiraterone acetate and prednisolone (combi-
55|nation therapy). The comparison was open-label,
56|because masking of the treatment assignment
57|was deemed impracticable. Eligible patients could
58|be assigned to any of the trial groups that were
59|open; we focus here on patients assigned con-
60|temporaneously to ADT alone or with abiraterone
61|and prednisolone.
62|Procedures
63|ADT was given for at least 2 years; radiotherapy
64|at 6 to 9 months after randomization was man-
65|datory for patients with node-negative, nonmeta-
66|static disease and optional for patients with node-
67|positive, nonmetastatic disease. Abiraterone
68|(1000 mg) with prednisolone (5 mg) was given
69|once daily. The treatment duration depended on
70|disease stage and intent for radical radiotherapy:
71|for patients with nonmetastatic disease with no
72|radiotherapy planned and for patients with meta-
73|static disease, treatment continued until PSA,
74|radiologic, or clinical progression or until an-
75|other treatment was started; for patients with
76|nonmetastatic disease with radiotherapy planned,
77|treatment was to continue for 2 years or until
78|any type of progression, whichever came first.
79|Dose modifications are described in the protocol.
80|Patients were assessed every 6 weeks during
81|the first 6 months, then every 12 weeks until
82|2 years, then every 6 months until 5 years, and
83|then annually; in addition, patients receiving
84|combination therapy were assessed at least every
85|3 months. Assessments included PSA testing and
86|ascertainment of adverse events; further tests
87|were conducted at the discretion of the treating
88|physician. The nadir PSA level (for the definition
89|of PSA progression) was defined as the lowest
90|level within 24 weeks after randomization. There
91|was no protocol-mandated imaging except at
92|baseline. Adverse events were assessed with the
93|use of the National Cancer Institute Common
94|Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (initial-
95|ly, version 3.0; later, version 4.0). Serious adverse
96|events and reactions were reported accordingly.
97|Statistical Analysis
98|The sample size was calculated with the use of
99|Stata nstage and predecessor programs that allow
100|for the design of multigroup, multistage trials.23
101|Assuming a median failure-free survival of 2 years
102|and a median overall survival between 4 and
103|5 years for ADT, we targeted a 25% relative dif-
104|ference between the combination group and the

4|ADT-alone group for both failure-free survival
5|(hazard ratio for treatment failure, 0.75) and
6|overall survival (hazard ratio for death, 0.75).
7|The main analysis for the comparison of combi-
8|nation therapy against control for survival could
9|be performed after the occurrence of approxi-
10|mately 267 deaths in the control group for 90%
11|power and a one-sided alpha level of 2.5%, after
12|we accounted for three intermediate lack-of-
13|benefit analyses of failure-free survival. An inde-
14|pendent data monitoring committee reviewed
15|accumulating data, guided by lack-of-benefit
16|stopping guidelines.
17|Data on patients without an event of interest
18|were censored when they were last known to be
19|event-free. The median follow-up was determined
20|through reversing death and censoring indica-
21|tors. Standard survival-analysis methods were
22|used to analyze time-to-event data in Stata soft-
23|ware, version 14, with Kaplan-Meier estimates
24|for survival curves and Cox proportional-hazards
25|models to estimate relative treatment effects.
26|These estimates were adjusted for stratification
27|factors (except randomizing center and ADT
28|method) and were stratified according to time
29|periods defined by corecruiting groups. A hazard
30|ratio of less than 1.00 favored the combination
31|group. The restricted mean survival time (restrict-
32|ed to 54 months) was calculated from flexible
33|parametric models (5 degrees of freedom). The
34|proportional-hazards assumption was tested; the
35|restricted mean survival time was emphasized in
36|the presence of nonproportionality. All the con-
37|fidence intervals are at the 95% level. Prespeci-
38|fied subgroup analyses looked at the consistency
39|of treatment effect according to stratification
40|factors, time period, categorized Gleason score,
41|and quintiles of PSA levels that were measured
42|before the initiation of long-term ADT. Key sub-
43|group analyses according to metastatic status
44|were prespecified. Exploratory analyses considered
45|prostate cancer-specific survival and progression-
46|free survival according to the age at random-
47|ization.
48|All the patients were included in the efficacy
49|analyses under their assigned treatment on an
50|intention-to-treat basis. For safety analyses, pa-
51|tients were grouped according to the treatment
52|that they started. In the analysis of the median
53|duration of abiraterone treatment, data were cen-
54|sored at the date of last contact with the patient
55|if the patient had not reported stopping the drug.
56|Results
57|Patients
58|Between November 15, 2011, and January 17,
59|2014, a total of 1917 consenting patients at 111
60|U.K. and 5 Swiss sites underwent randomization
61|(957 to ADT alone and 960 to combination
62|therapy). Data were frozen on February 10, 2017.
63|The flow of patients through the trial is shown
64|in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix,
65|available at NEJM.org; the baseline characteris-
66|tics of the patients are shown in Table 1, and in
67|Table S1 in the Supplementary Appendix. The
68|median PSA level was 53 ng per milliliter. The
69|median follow-up was 40 months.
70|Treatment
71|The median time from randomization to the ini-
72|tiation of abiraterone was 1.3 weeks, and the
73|median time from the initiation of ADT to the
74|initiation of abiraterone was 8.0 weeks (most pa-
75|tients started ADT before randomization) (Table
76|S2 in the Supplementary Appendix). Of the 960
77|patients in the combination group, 10 (1%) did
78|not receive abiraterone, mostly because they de-
79|clined treatment. The median duration of abira
80|terone treatment was 23.7 months in the patients
81|for whom the duration was capped at 2 years
82|(67% reported stopping for treatment comple-
83|tion) and 33.2 months in the patients who could
84|continue through progression (51% reported per-
85|manent stopping for progression and 20% for
86|excessive toxic effects) (Table S2 and Fig. S2 in
87|the Supplementary Appendix). A total of 265
88|patients (28%) had not yet permanently stopped
89|treatment with abiraterone at the time of this
90|report.
91|The planned rate of use of radiotherapy was
92|41% in the combination group and in the ADT-
93|alone group. The reported rate of use of radio-
94|therapy was 39% in the combination group and
95|40% in the ADT-alone group.
96|Overall Survival
97|There were 184 deaths in the combination group
98|and 262 in the ADT-alone group. There was
99|strong evidence of a survival advantage in the
100|combination group, with a 3-year survival of
101|83% as compared with 76% in the ADT-alone
102|group (hazard ratio for death, 0.63; 95% confi-
103|dence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.76; P<0.001) (Fig. 1A).

6|randomization. A preplanned subgroup analysis
7|of 1002 patients with metastatic disease at entry
8|included 368 deaths (Fig. 1C). The same com-
9|parisons in patients without metastatic disease
10|at randomization are immature, currently with
11|78 deaths in total (Fig. 1E). There was no evi-
12|dence of heterogeneity of effect in other sub-
13|groups (Fig. 2A).
14|Failure-free Survival
15|There were 248 events of treatment failure (radio-
16|logic, clinical, or PSA progression or death from
17|prostate cancer) in the combination group and 535
18|in the ADT-alone group. The 3-year failure-free
19|survival was 75% in the combination group and
20|45% in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for treat-
21|ment failure, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.34; P<0.001)
22|(Fig. 1B). There was evidence of nonproportional
23|hazards (P = 0.001), so we present restricted
24|mean failure-free survival time: 43.9 months in
25|the combination group and 30.0 months in the
26|ADT-alone group in the first 54 months after
27|randomization, a difference of 13.9 months
28|(95% CI, 12.3 to 15.4). The effect of abiraterone
29|on failure-free survival was noted in all sub-
30|groups (Fig. 1D and 1F and Fig. 2B).
31|Other Efficacy Outcome Measures
32|There were 198 events of radiologic or clinical
33|progression or death from prostate cancer in the
34|combination group and 379 in the ADT-alone
35|group. The 3-year progression-free survival was
36|80% in the combination group and 62% in the
37|ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for clinical or
38|radiologic progression or death from prostate
39|cancer, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.47; P<0.001) (Fig.
40|S3 in the Supplementary Appendix). There were
41|113 symptomatic skeletal events reported so far
42|in the combination group and 203 in the ADT-
43|alone group. The 3-year rate without symptom-
44|atic skeletal events was 88% in the combination
45|group and 78% in the ADT-alone group (hazard
46|ratio for symptomatic skeletal events, 0.46; 95%
47|CI, 0.37 to 0.58; P<0.001) (Fig. S4A in the Supple-
48|mentary Appendix). This difference was most
49|marked in the subgroup of patients with meta-
50|static disease (Fig. S4B in the Supplementary
51|Appendix). A total of 140 of the 184 deaths in
52|the combination group (76%) and 216 of the 262
53|deaths in the ADT-alone group (82%) were attrib-
54|uted to prostate cancer on central review. The
55|competing-risks subhazard ratio for death from
56|prostate cancer was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.47 to 0.72).
57|Exploratory Analyses
58|Exploratory analyses that considered the outcomes
59|of progression-free and prostate cancer-specific
60|survival within subgroups of age at randomiza-
61|tion suggested a favorable treatment effect re-
62|gardless of age; proportionally fewer events were
63|noted in older patients. In patients younger than
64|70 years of age, there were 113 events of radio-
65|logic or clinical progression or death from pros-
66|tate cancer in the combination group and 263 in
67|the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio, 0.36; 95% CI,
68|0.29 to 0.45); in patients 70 years of age or older,
69|there were 65 events in the combination group
70|and 116 in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio,
71|0.50; 95% CI, 0.37 to 0.68; P = 0.10 for interac-
72|tion). In patients younger than 70 years of age,
73|there were 93 deaths from prostate cancer in the
74|combination group and 154 in the ADT-alone
75|group (subhazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.39 to
76|0.66); in patients 70 years of age or older, there
77|were 47 deaths from prostate cancer in the com-
78|bination group and 62 in the ADT-alone group
79|(subhazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.17;
80|P = 0.08 for interaction).
81|Adverse Events
82|Patients in the safety population who reported
83|adverse events of grade 3 or higher during their
84|entire time in the trial numbered 443 of 948
85|(47%) in the combination group and 315 of 960
86|(33%) in the ADT-alone group (Table 2). There
87|were 12 grade 5 adverse events, including 9 in
88|the combination group (2 events of pneumonia
89|[1 including sepsis], 2 events of stroke, and 1 event
90|each of dyspnea, lower respiratory tract infection,
91|liver failure, pulmonary hemorrhage, and chest
92|infection) and 3 in the ADT-alone group (2 events
93|of myocardial infarction and 1 event of broncho-
94|pneumonia). Among the 1476 patients in the
95|safety population in whom progression had not
96|occurred within the first year, the prevalence of
97|adverse events of grade 3 or higher was 15% in
98|the combination group and 11% in the ADT-
99|alone group. The main additional adverse events
100|over and above the control therapy were hyper-
101|tension, mild increases in aminotransferase levels,
102|and respiratory disorders. Further details, includ-

8|Treatment after Progression
9|There are emerging differences in the therapies
10|used at relapse (Fig. 3, and Table S3 in the Sup-
11|plementary Appendix). The median time from
12|relapse to life-prolonging therapy for castration-
13|resistant prostate cancer (abiraterone, enzaluta
14|mide, docetaxel, cabazitaxel, or radium-223) or
15|any subsequent therapy was similar in the two
16|groups, but absolute numbers of patients report-
17|ing life-prolonging or any treatment after pro-
18|gression were higher in the ADT-alone group
19|than in the combination group (ADT-alone group,
20|310 and 477, respectively, of 957 patients; com-
21|bination group, 131 and 196, respectively, of
22|960 patients). The use of abiraterone at relapse
23|in patients who received abiraterone as primary
24|therapy was lower in patients in the combination
25|group than in patients in the ADT-alone group;
26|patients in the combination group could con-
27|tinue abiraterone beyond the first event of radio-
28|logic, clinical, or PSA progression until all three
29|protocol-defined progression types were reached.
30|The rate of docetaxel use was proportionately
31|higher in the combination group than in the
32|ADT-alone group. Because 1471 of the men (77%)
33|in this comparison remain alive, these data will
34|evolve with time as more patients have a relapse
35|and receive further treatments.
36|Discussion
37|STAMPEDE is a multigroup, multistage platform
38|trial protocol investigating the efficacy of addi-
39|tional therapy at the time of inception of primary
40|ADT in men with newly diagnosed, locally ad-
41|vanced, or metastatic disease or in those with
42|relapsing disease and poor prognostic features.
43|This is the sixth comparison in the trial for which
44|we are reporting survival data15,16,24-27 and the first
45|comparison incorporated after trial initiation.22
46|The use of ADT plus abiraterone and predniso-
47|lone as compared with ADT alone was associat-
48|ed with a 71% relative improvement in the time
49|to treatment failure, which translated into a 37%
50|difference in overall survival. These findings were
51|consistent in patients with metastatic disease
52|and those with nonmetastatic disease, although
53|most deaths have occurred in the patients with
54|metastatic disease. The between-group difference
55|in survival among the patients with nonmeta-
56|static disease, which is underpinned by a large
57|difference in failure-free survival, occurred even
58|though abiraterone was administered for 2 years
59|or less in this group.
60|There was good adherence to abiraterone,
61|which was associated with acceptable adverse-
62|event rates, with most patients stopping therapy
63|owing to the completion of planned therapy or
64|protocol-defined progression rather than toxic
65|effects. Adverse events were in line with previous
66|experience in castration-resistant prostate can-
67|cer,4,5,21 despite the longer absolute duration of
68|therapy, particularly in the patients with meta-
69|static disease. Nearly 300 patients are still re-
70|ceiving treatment. Few patients stopped treat-
71|ment because of side effects, but there were
72|more grade 3 to 5 adverse events reported in the
73|combination group than in the ADT-alone group.
74|The lower dose of prednisolone that was used
75|does not seem to have influenced the rate of
76|pharmacologically relevant severe adverse events,
77|such as hypertension or hypokalemia.20
78|The strengths of the comparison in this trial
79|include broad recruitment through an academic
80|network (116 centers, including most U.K. on-
81|cology centers, in collaboration with the Swiss
82|Group for Clinical Cancer Research) encompass-
83|ing a wide range of disease states. The size of
84|the trial permits some examination of inter
85|actions, including those with other treatments
86|known to be effective (e.g., radiotherapy) and
87|prognostic factors used for stratification at ran-
88|domization. Effects in all subgroups were simi-
89|lar, with no evidence of heterogeneity. The appar-
90|ent inconsistency in survival-effect size in men
91|70 years of age or older is probably an artifact
92|arising from a small number of events; the ab-
93|solute difference is only 8 deaths (74 in the
94|combination group and 82 in the ADT-alone
95|group). The result is complicated by a higher risk

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the sequence method. A truncated search does not establish that the method is absent.

Abiraterone for Prostate Cancer
ards (P = 0.31) or of heterogeneity of the treat-
ment effect according to metastatic status at
randomization. A preplanned subgroup analysis
of 1002 patients with metastatic disease at entry
included 368 deaths (Fig. 1C). The same com-
parisons in patients without metastatic disease
at randomization are immature, currently with
78 deaths in total (Fig. 1E). There was no evi-
dence of heterogeneity of effect in other sub-
groups (Fig. 2A).
Failure-free Survival
There were 248 events of treatment failure (radio-
logic, clinical, or PSA progression or death from
prostate cancer) in the combination group and 535
in the ADT-alone group. The 3-year failure-free
survival was 75% in the combination group and
45% in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for treat-
ment failure, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.34; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). There was evidence of nonproportional
hazards (P = 0.001), so we present restricted
mean failure-free survival time: 43.9 months in
the combination group and 30.0 months in the
ADT-alone group in the first 54 months after
randomization, a difference of 13.9 months
(95% CI, 12.3 to 15.4). The effect of abiraterone
on failure-free survival was noted in all sub-
groups (Fig. 1D and 1F and Fig. 2B).
Other Efficacy Outcome Measures
There were 198 events of radiologic or clinical
progression or death from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 379 in the ADT-alone
group. The 3-year progression-free survival was
80% in the combination group and 62% in the
ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for clinical or
radiologic progression or death from prostate
cancer, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.47; P<0.001) (Fig.
S3 in the Supplementary Appendix). There were
113 symptomatic skeletal events reported so far
in the combination group and 203 in the ADT-
alone group. The 3-year rate without symptom-
atic skeletal events was 88% in the combination
group and 78% in the ADT-alone group (hazard
ratio for symptomatic skeletal events, 0.46; 95%
CI, 0.37 to 0.58; P<0.001) (Fig. S4A in the Supple-
mentary Appendix). This difference was most
marked in the subgroup of patients with meta-
static disease (Fig. S4B in the Supplementary
Appendix). A total of 140 of the 184 deaths in
the combination group (76%) and 216 of the 262
deaths in the ADT-alone group (82%) were attrib-
uted to prostate cancer on central review. The
competing-risks subhazard ratio for death from
prostate cancer was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.47 to 0.72).
Exploratory Analyses
Exploratory analyses that considered the outcomes
of progression-free and prostate cancer-specific
survival within subgroups of age at randomiza-
tion suggested a favorable treatment effect re-
gardless of age; proportionally fewer events were
noted in older patients. In patients younger than
70 years of age, there were 113 events of radio-
logic or clinical progression or death from pros-
tate cancer in the combination group and 263 in
the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio, 0.36; 95% CI,
0.29 to 0.45); in patients 70 years of age or older,
there were 65 events in the combination group
and 116 in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio,
0.50; 95% CI, 0.37 to 0.68; P = 0.10 for interac-
tion). In patients younger than 70 years of age,
there were 93 deaths from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 154 in the ADT-alone
group (subhazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.39 to
0.66); in patients 70 years of age or older, there
were 47 deaths from prostate cancer in the com-
bination group and 62 in the ADT-alone group
(subhazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.17;
P = 0.08 for interaction).
Adverse Events
Patients in the safety population who reported
adverse events of grade 3 or higher during their
entire time in the trial numbered 443 of 948

The main analysis for the comparison of combi-
nation therapy against control for survival could
be performed after the occurrence of approxi-
mately 267 deaths in the control group for 90%
power and a one-sided alpha level of 2.5%, after
we accounted for three intermediate lack-of-
benefit analyses of failure-free survival. An inde-
pendent data monitoring committee reviewed
accumulating data, guided by lack-of-benefit
stopping guidelines.
Data on patients without an event of interest
were censored when they were last known to be
event-free. The median follow-up was determined
through reversing death and censoring indica-
tors. Standard survival-analysis methods were
used to analyze time-to-event data in Stata soft-
ware, version 14, with Kaplan-Meier estimates
for survival curves and Cox proportional-hazards
models to estimate relative treatment effects.
These estimates were adjusted for stratification
factors (except randomizing center and ADT
method) and were stratified according to time
periods defined by corecruiting groups. A hazard
ratio of less than 1.00 favored the combination
group. The restricted mean survival time (restrict-
ed to 54 months) was calculated from flexible
parametric models (5 degrees of freedom). The
proportional-hazards assumption was tested; the
restricted mean survival time was emphasized in
the presence of nonproportionality. All the con-
fidence intervals are at the 95% level. Prespeci-
fied subgroup analyses looked at the consistency
of treatment effect according to stratification
factors, time period, categorized Gleason score,
and quintiles of PSA levels that were measured
before the initiation of long-term ADT. Key sub-
group analyses according to metastatic status
were prespecified. Exploratory analyses considered
prostate cancer-specific survival and progression-
free survival according to the age at random-
ization.
All the patients were included in the efficacy
analyses under their assigned treatment on an
intention-to-treat basis. For safety analyses, pa-
tients were grouped according to the treatment
that they started. In the analysis of the median
duration of abiraterone treatment, data were cen-
sored at the date of last contact with the patient
if the patient had not reported stopping the drug.
Results
Patients
Between November 15, 2011, and January 17,
2014, a total of 1917 consenting patients at 111
U.K. and 5 Swiss sites underwent randomization
(957 to ADT alone and 960 to combination
therapy). Data were frozen on February 10, 2017.
The flow of patients through the trial is shown
in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix,
available at NEJM.org; the baseline characteris-
tics of the patients are shown in Table 1, and in
Table S1 in the Supplementary Appendix. The
median PSA level was 53 ng per milliliter. The
median follow-up was 40 months.
Treatment
The median time from randomization to the ini-
tiation of abiraterone was 1.3 weeks, and the
median time from the initiation of ADT to the
initiation of abiraterone was 8.0 weeks (most pa-
tients started ADT before randomization) (Table
S2 in the Supplementary Appendix). Of the 960
patients in the combination group, 10 (1%) did
not receive abiraterone, mostly because they de-
clined treatment. The median duration of abira
terone treatment was 23.7 months in the patients
for whom the duration was capped at 2 years
(67% reported stopping for treatment comple-
tion) and 33.2 months in the patients who could
continue through progression (51% reported per-
manent stopping for progression and 20% for
excessive toxic effects) (Table S2 and Fig. S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). A total of 265
patients (28%) had not yet permanently stopped
treatment with abiraterone at the time of this
report.
The planned rate of use of radiotherapy was
41% in the combination group and in the ADT-
alone group. The reported rate of use of radio-
therapy was 39% in the combination group and
40% in the ADT-alone group.

There were 184 deaths in the combination group
and 262 in the ADT-alone group. There was
strong evidence of a survival advantage in the
combination group, with a 3-year survival of
83% as compared with 76% in the ADT-alone
group (hazard ratio for death, 0.63; 95% confi-
dence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.76; P<0.001) (Fig. 1A).

The baseline table shows similar randomized group sizes (957 vs 960) and broadly similar prognostic characteristics: median age and performance status are equal, and disease stage, Gleason score, planned radiotherapy, and ADT type have only small percentage differences. The table does not suggest a randomization problem; the observed variations are compatible with chance.

ment effect according to metastatic status at
randomization. A preplanned subgroup analysis
of 1002 patients with metastatic disease at entry
included 368 deaths (Fig. 1C). The same com-
parisons in patients without metastatic disease
at randomization are immature, currently with
78 deaths in total (Fig. 1E). There was no evi-
dence of heterogeneity of effect in other sub-
groups (Fig. 2A).
Failure-free Survival
There were 248 events of treatment failure (radio-
logic, clinical, or PSA progression or death from
prostate cancer) in the combination group and 535
in the ADT-alone group. The 3-year failure-free
survival was 75% in the combination group and
45% in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for treat-
ment failure, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.34; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). There was evidence of nonproportional
hazards (P = 0.001), so we present restricted
mean failure-free survival time: 43.9 months in
the combination group and 30.0 months in the
ADT-alone group in the first 54 months after
randomization, a difference of 13.9 months
(95% CI, 12.3 to 15.4). The effect of abiraterone
on failure-free survival was noted in all sub-
groups (Fig. 1D and 1F and Fig. 2B).
Other Efficacy Outcome Measures
There were 198 events of radiologic or clinical
progression or death from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 379 in the ADT-alone
group. The 3-year progression-free survival was
80% in the combination group and 62% in the
ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for clinical or
radiologic progression or death from prostate
cancer, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.47; P<0.001) (Fig.
S3 in the Supplementary Appendix). There were
113 symptomatic skeletal events reported so far
in the combination group and 203 in the ADT-
alone group. The 3-year rate without symptom-
atic skeletal events was 88% in the combination
group and 78% in the ADT-alone group (hazard
ratio for symptomatic skeletal events, 0.46; 95%
CI, 0.37 to 0.58; P<0.001) (Fig. S4A in the Supple-
mentary Appendix). This difference was most
marked in the subgroup of patients with meta-
static disease (Fig. S4B in the Supplementary
Appendix). A total of 140 of the 184 deaths in
the combination group (76%) and 216 of the 262
deaths in the ADT-alone group (82%) were attrib-
uted to prostate cancer on central review. The
competing-risks subhazard ratio for death from
prostate cancer was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.47 to 0.72).
Exploratory Analyses
Exploratory analyses that considered the outcomes
of progression-free and prostate cancer-specific
survival within subgroups of age at randomiza-
tion suggested a favorable treatment effect re-
gardless of age; proportionally fewer events were
noted in older patients. In patients younger than
70 years of age, there were 113 events of radio-
logic or clinical progression or death from pros-
tate cancer in the combination group and 263 in
the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio, 0.36; 95% CI,
0.29 to 0.45); in patients 70 years of age or older,
there were 65 events in the combination group
and 116 in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio,
0.50; 95% CI, 0.37 to 0.68; P = 0.10 for interac-
tion). In patients younger than 70 years of age,
there were 93 deaths from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 154 in the ADT-alone
group (subhazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.39 to
0.66); in patients 70 years of age or older, there
were 47 deaths from prostate cancer in the com-
bination group and 62 in the ADT-alone group
(subhazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.17;
P = 0.08 for interaction).
Adverse Events
Patients in the safety population who reported
adverse events of grade 3 or higher during their
entire time in the trial numbered 443 of 948
(47%) in the combination group and 315 of 960
(33%) in the ADT-alone group (Table 2). There
were 12 grade 5 adverse events, including 9 in
the combination group (2 events of pneumonia
[1 including sepsis], 2 events of stroke, and 1 event
each of dyspnea, lower respiratory tract infection,
liver failure, pulmonary hemorrhage, and chest
infection) and 3 in the ADT-alone group (2 events
of myocardial infarction and 1 event of broncho-
pneumonia). Among the 1476 patients in the
safety population in whom progression had not
occurred within the first year, the prevalence of
adverse events of grade 3 or higher was 15% in
the combination group and 11% in the ADT-
alone group. The main additional adverse events
over and above the control therapy were hyper-
tension, mild increases in aminotransferase levels,
and respiratory disorders. Further details, includ-

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

The main analysis for the comparison of combi-

Data on patients without an event of interest
were censored when they were last known to be
event-free. The median follow-up was determined
through reversing death and censoring indica-
tors. Standard survival-analysis methods were
used to analyze time-to-event data in Stata soft-
ware, version 14, with Kaplan-Meier estimates
for survival curves and Cox proportional-hazards
models to estimate relative treatment effects.
These estimates were adjusted for stratification
factors (except randomizing center and ADT
method) and were stratified according to time
periods defined by corecruiting groups. A hazard
ratio of less than 1.00 favored the combination
group. The restricted mean survival time (restrict-
ed to 54 months) was calculated from flexible
parametric models (5 degrees of freedom). The
proportional-hazards assumption was tested; the
restricted mean survival time was emphasized in
the presence of nonproportionality. All the con-
fidence intervals are at the 95% level. Prespeci-
fied subgroup analyses looked at the consistency
of treatment effect according to stratification
factors, time period, categorized Gleason score,
and quintiles of PSA levels that were measured
before the initiation of long-term ADT. Key sub-
group analyses according to metastatic status
were prespecified. Exploratory analyses considered
prostate cancer-specific survival and progression-
free survival according to the age at random-

All the patients were included in the efficacy
analyses under their assigned treatment on an
intention-to-treat basis. For safety analyses, pa-
tients were grouped according to the treatment
that they started. In the analysis of the median

sored at the date of last contact with the patient
if the patient had not reported stopping the drug.

Patients
Between November 15, 2011, and January 17,
2014, a total of 1917 consenting patients at 111
U.K. and 5 Swiss sites underwent randomization
(957 to ADT alone and 960 to combination
therapy). Data were frozen on February 10, 2017.
The flow of patients through the trial is shown
in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix,
available at NEJM.org; the baseline characteris-

Table S1 in the Supplementary Appendix. The
median PSA level was 53 ng per milliliter. The
median follow-up was 40 months.

The median time from randomization to the ini-
tiation of abiraterone was 1.3 weeks, and the
median time from the initiation of ADT to the

answers.justification: The report explicitly says the comparison was open-label because masking treatment assignment was considered impracticable. Participants therefore knew their assigned intervention.
The same open-label statement applies to the clinicians and trial personnel delivering the distinct regimens; treatment assignment was not masked.

Ten of 960 assigned to combination therapy did not receive abiraterone, mostly because they declined treatment. The protocol recognizes a participant's right to withdraw and allows stopping treatment after withdrawal of treatment consent. This limited non-initiation is consistent with ordinary participant refusal and is not reported as a trial-context-caused, protocol-inconsistent deviation; the reason for each refusal is not specified, so I use probably no.
unknowns: The report does not give the individual reasons for all ten non-initiation decisions or link them to the open-label trial context.

This does not estimate the approved assignment effect in randomized groups.

questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

answer_anchors.text: Outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
Outcome data were not available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
The report provides no information about the extent of missing outcome data.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. ards (P = 0.31) or of heterogeneity of the treat-
ment effect according to metastatic status at
randomization. A preplanned subgroup analysis
of 1002 patients with metastatic disease at entry
included 368 deaths (Fig. 1C). The same com-
parisons in patients without metastatic disease
at randomization are immature, currently with
78 deaths in total (Fig. 1E). There was no evi-
dence of heterogeneity of effect in other sub-
groups (Fig. 2A).
Failure-free Survival
There were 248 events of treatment failure (radio-
logic, clinical, or PSA progression or death from
prostate cancer) in the combination group and 535
in the ADT-alone group. The 3-year failure-free
survival was 75% in the combination group and
45% in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for treat-
ment failure, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.34; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). There was evidence of nonproportional
hazards (P = 0.001), so we present restricted
mean failure-free survival time: 43.9 months in
the combination group and 30.0 months in the
ADT-alone group in the first 54 months after
randomization, a difference of 13.9 months
(95% CI, 12.3 to 15.4). The effect of abiraterone
on failure-free survival was noted in all sub-
groups (Fig. 1D and 1F and Fig. 2B).
Other Efficacy Outcome Measures
There were 198 events of radiologic or clinical
progression or death from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 379 in the ADT-alone
group. The 3-year progression-free survival was
80% in the combination group and 62% in the
ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for clinical or
radiologic progression or death from prostate
cancer, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.47; P<0.001) (Fig.
S3 in the Supplementary Appendix). There were
113 symptomatic skeletal events reported so far
in the combination group and 203 in the ADT-
alone group. The 3-year rate without symptom-
atic skeletal events was 88% in the combination
group and 78% in the ADT-alone group (hazard
ratio for symptomatic skeletal events, 0.46; 95%
CI, 0.37 to 0.58; P<0.001) (Fig. S4A in the Supple-
mentary Appendix). This difference was most
marked in the subgroup of patients with meta-
static disease (Fig. S4B in the Supplementary
Appendix). A total of 140 of the 184 deaths in
the combination group (76%) and 216 of the 262
deaths in the ADT-alone group (82%) were attrib-
uted to prostate cancer on central review. The
competing-risks subhazard ratio for death from
prostate cancer was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.47 to 0.72).
Exploratory Analyses
Exploratory analyses that considered the outcomes
of progression-free and prostate cancer-specific
survival within subgroups of age at randomiza-
tion suggested a favorable treatment effect re-
gardless of age; proportionally fewer events were
noted in older patients. In patients younger than
70 years of age, there were 113 events of radio-
logic or clinical progression or death from pros-
tate cancer in the combination group and 263 in
the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio, 0.36; 95% CI,
0.29 to 0.45); in patients 70 years of age or older,
there were 65 events in the combination group
and 116 in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio,
0.50; 95% CI, 0.37 to 0.68; P = 0.10 for interac-
tion). In patients younger than 70 years of age,
there were 93 deaths from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 154 in the ADT-alone
group (subhazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.39 to
0.66); in patients 70 years of age or older, there
were 47 deaths from prostate cancer in the com-
bination group and 62 in the ADT-alone group
(subhazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.17;
P = 0.08 for interaction).
Adverse Events
Patients in the safety population who reported
adverse events of grade 3 or higher during their
entire time in the trial numbered 443 of 948
(47%) in the combination group and 315 of 960
(33%) in the ADT-alone group (Table 2). There
were 12 grade 5 adverse events, including 9 in
the combination group (2 events of pneumonia
[1 including sepsis], 2 events of stroke, and 1 event
each of dyspnea, lower respiratory tract infection,
liver failure, pulmonary hemorrhage, and chest
infection) and 3 in the ADT-alone group (2 events
of myocardial infarction and 1 event of broncho-
pneumonia). Among the 1476 patients in the
safety population in whom progression had not
occurred within the first year, the prevalence of
adverse events of grade 3 or higher was 15% in
the combination group and 11% in the ADT-
alone group. The main additional adverse events
over and above the control therapy were hyper-
tension, mild increases in aminotransferase levels,

The main analysis for the comparison of combi-
nation therapy against control for survival could
be performed after the occurrence of approxi-
mately 267 deaths in the control group for 90%
power and a one-sided alpha level of 2.5%, after
we accounted for three intermediate lack-of-
benefit analyses of failure-free survival. An inde-
pendent data monitoring committee reviewed
accumulating data, guided by lack-of-benefit
stopping guidelines.
Data on patients without an event of interest
were censored when they were last known to be
event-free. The median follow-up was determined
through reversing death and censoring indica-
tors. Standard survival-analysis methods were
used to analyze time-to-event data in Stata soft-
ware, version 14, with Kaplan-Meier estimates
for survival curves and Cox proportional-hazards
models to estimate relative treatment effects.
These estimates were adjusted for stratification
factors (except randomizing center and ADT
method) and were stratified according to time
periods defined by corecruiting groups. A hazard
ratio of less than 1.00 favored the combination
group. The restricted mean survival time (restrict-
ed to 54 months) was calculated from flexible
parametric models (5 degrees of freedom). The
proportional-hazards assumption was tested; the
restricted mean survival time was emphasized in
the presence of nonproportionality. All the con-
fidence intervals are at the 95% level. Prespeci-
fied subgroup analyses looked at the consistency
of treatment effect according to stratification
factors, time period, categorized Gleason score,
and quintiles of PSA levels that were measured
before the initiation of long-term ADT. Key sub-
group analyses according to metastatic status
were prespecified. Exploratory analyses considered
prostate cancer-specific survival and progression-
free survival according to the age at random-
ization.
All the patients were included in the efficacy
analyses under their assigned treatment on an
intention-to-treat basis. For safety analyses, pa-
tients were grouped according to the treatment
that they started. In the analysis of the median
duration of abiraterone treatment, data were cen-
sored at the date of last contact with the patient
if the patient had not reported stopping the drug.
Results
Patients
Between November 15, 2011, and January 17,
2014, a total of 1917 consenting patients at 111
U.K. and 5 Swiss sites underwent randomization
(957 to ADT alone and 960 to combination
therapy). Data were frozen on February 10, 2017.
The flow of patients through the trial is shown
in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix,
available at NEJM.org; the baseline characteris-
tics of the patients are shown in Table 1, and in
Table S1 in the Supplementary Appendix. The
median PSA level was 53 ng per milliliter. The
median follow-up was 40 months.
Treatment
The median time from randomization to the ini-
tiation of abiraterone was 1.3 weeks, and the
median time from the initiation of ADT to the
initiation of abiraterone was 8.0 weeks (most pa-
tients started ADT before randomization) (Table
S2 in the Supplementary Appendix). Of the 960
patients in the combination group, 10 (1%) did
not receive abiraterone, mostly because they de-
clined treatment. The median duration of abira
terone treatment was 23.7 months in the patients
for whom the duration was capped at 2 years
(67% reported stopping for treatment comple-
tion) and 33.2 months in the patients who could
continue through progression (51% reported per-
manent stopping for progression and 20% for
excessive toxic effects) (Table S2 and Fig. S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). A total of 265
patients (28%) had not yet permanently stopped
treatment with abiraterone at the time of this
report.
The planned rate of use of radiotherapy was
41% in the combination group and in the ADT-
alone group. The reported rate of use of radio-
therapy was 39% in the combination group and
40% in the ADT-alone group.

There were 184 deaths in the combination group
and 262 in the ADT-alone group. There was
strong evidence of a survival advantage in the
combination group, with a 3-year survival of
83% as compared with 76% in the ADT-alone

dence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.76; P<0.001) (Fig. 1A).

item.text: The main report’s intention-to-treat safety table gives outcome-analysis counts of 953/957 and 955/960, with grade 3–5 events reported in both groups. That leaves nine randomized participants outside the reported safety analysis (about 0.5%); the report does not explain their status. I’ll treat availability as probably near-complete, with that gap recorded as unknown.

answers.justification: For the intention-to-treat population, Table 2 reports 953 of 957 ADT-alone and 955 of 960 combination participants in the safety analysis, and gives adverse-event outcomes for those groups. This is 1,908/1,917 (99.5%) of randomized participants. I infer outcome data were available for nearly all; even if all nine outside the safety analysis had missing data, that fraction is too small to materially change this common grade 3–5 outcome. The report does not account for those nine individually, so the conclusion is probable rather than certain.
unknowns: The report does not state why four ADT-alone and five combination participants were not in the intention-to-treat safety analysis or explicitly describe their adverse-event data availability.

questions.wording: Was the method of measuring the outcome inappropriate?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ if the method of measuring the outcome is inappropriate, for example because it is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the measurement instrument has been demonstrated to have poor validity.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 54, Box 10, signalling question 4.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate for the outcome, including validity and sensitivity to plausible intervention effects.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the method is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the instrument has demonstrated poor validity. Validity and sensitivity are distinct from detection opportunity, assessor identity or awareness, and whether knowledge influenced assessment. Do not assess whether choosing the outcome itself was sensible.
evidence_needed: The measurement method's sensitivity to plausible effects and evidence of instrument validity for this outcome.

For a mixed objective and subjective composite, inspect each component that can determine the approved event; objective components do not establish validity or influence conclusions for a subjective component.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when appropriateness of the measurement method cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The measurement method is unsuitable, insensitive, or poorly valid for this outcome.
The measurement method is appropriate for this outcome.

considerations: For pre-specified outcomes the answer will usually be no or probably no.

Measurement susceptibility concerns whether the method can validly and sensitively measure this outcome. It is distinct from assessor awareness, detection opportunity, and whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced assessment.

A standardized instrument can still involve judgment in elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment. Preserve component-specific Evidence and uncertainty for mixed objective and subjective components.

ards (P = 0.31) or of heterogeneity of the treat-
ment effect according to metastatic status at
randomization. A preplanned subgroup analysis
of 1002 patients with metastatic disease at entry
included 368 deaths (Fig. 1C). The same com-
parisons in patients without metastatic disease
at randomization are immature, currently with
78 deaths in total (Fig. 1E). There was no evi-
dence of heterogeneity of effect in other sub-
groups (Fig. 2A).
Failure-free Survival
There were 248 events of treatment failure (radio-
logic, clinical, or PSA progression or death from
prostate cancer) in the combination group and 535
in the ADT-alone group. The 3-year failure-free
survival was 75% in the combination group and
45% in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for treat-
ment failure, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.34; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). There was evidence of nonproportional
hazards (P = 0.001), so we present restricted
mean failure-free survival time: 43.9 months in
the combination group and 30.0 months in the
ADT-alone group in the first 54 months after
randomization, a difference of 13.9 months
(95% CI, 12.3 to 15.4). The effect of abiraterone
on failure-free survival was noted in all sub-
groups (Fig. 1D and 1F and Fig. 2B).
Other Efficacy Outcome Measures
There were 198 events of radiologic or clinical
progression or death from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 379 in the ADT-alone
group. The 3-year progression-free survival was
80% in the combination group and 62% in the
ADT-alone group (hazard ratio for clinical or
radiologic progression or death from prostate
cancer, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.47; P<0.001) (Fig.
S3 in the Supplementary Appendix). There were
113 symptomatic skeletal events reported so far
in the combination group and 203 in the ADT-
alone group. The 3-year rate without symptom-
atic skeletal events was 88% in the combination
group and 78% in the ADT-alone group (hazard
ratio for symptomatic skeletal events, 0.46; 95%
CI, 0.37 to 0.58; P<0.001) (Fig. S4A in the Supple-
mentary Appendix). This difference was most
marked in the subgroup of patients with meta-
static disease (Fig. S4B in the Supplementary
Appendix). A total of 140 of the 184 deaths in
the combination group (76%) and 216 of the 262
deaths in the ADT-alone group (82%) were attrib-
uted to prostate cancer on central review. The
competing-risks subhazard ratio for death from
prostate cancer was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.47 to 0.72).
Exploratory Analyses
Exploratory analyses that considered the outcomes
of progression-free and prostate cancer-specific
survival within subgroups of age at randomiza-
tion suggested a favorable treatment effect re-
gardless of age; proportionally fewer events were
noted in older patients. In patients younger than
70 years of age, there were 113 events of radio-
logic or clinical progression or death from pros-
tate cancer in the combination group and 263 in
the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio, 0.36; 95% CI,
0.29 to 0.45); in patients 70 years of age or older,
there were 65 events in the combination group
and 116 in the ADT-alone group (hazard ratio,
0.50; 95% CI, 0.37 to 0.68; P = 0.10 for interac-
tion). In patients younger than 70 years of age,
there were 93 deaths from prostate cancer in the
combination group and 154 in the ADT-alone
group (subhazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.39 to
0.66); in patients 70 years of age or older, there
were 47 deaths from prostate cancer in the com-
bination group and 62 in the ADT-alone group
(subhazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.17;
P = 0.08 for interaction).
Adverse Events
Patients in the safety population who reported
adverse events of grade 3 or higher during their
entire time in the trial numbered 443 of 948
(47%) in the combination group and 315 of 960
(33%) in the ADT-alone group (Table 2). There
were 12 grade 5 adverse events, including 9 in
the combination group (2 events of pneumonia
[1 including sepsis], 2 events of stroke, and 1 event
each of dyspnea, lower respiratory tract infection,
liver failure, pulmonary hemorrhage, and chest
infection) and 3 in the ADT-alone group (2 events
of myocardial infarction and 1 event of broncho-
pneumonia). Among the 1476 patients in the
safety population in whom progression had not
occurred within the first year, the prevalence of
adverse events of grade 3 or higher was 15% in
the combination group and 11% in the ADT-
alone group. The main additional adverse events
over and above the control therapy were hyper-
tension, mild increases in aminotransferase levels,
and respiratory disorders. Further details, includ-

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

considerations: Compare actual methods and detection opportunities. Assessor awareness or possible reporting influence alone does not establish a between-group method difference; assess awareness and influence in 4.3 to 4.5.

Detection opportunity is the chance an outcome could be identified or recorded, including passive ascertainment or intervention-related visits. Keep it separate from measurement susceptibility (4.1) and from who knew the assignment (4.3).
A different visit schedule or passive collection is not enough on its own: explain how it could make the approved outcome more or less likely to be detected in one group.
Neutral paired control: equal ascertainment schedules and intervention-created additional visits differ only in detection opportunity; do not turn that contrast into an automatic risk label.
questions.decision_rule: Comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points. Consider diagnostic detection bias from passive collection and additional healthcare visits caused by an intervention, but identify the pathway by which a different detection opportunity could change ascertainment before judging its severity.
evidence_needed: Methods, thresholds, timing, and opportunities for outcome ascertainment in each intervention group, plus the pathway connecting any opportunity difference to differential detection.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when comparability of measurement or ascertainment cannot be assessed.

This asks only whether the relevant assessor knew assignment. It does not establish that the measurement was susceptible to bias, that detection opportunities differed, or that knowledge likely changed the assessment; those are separate questions.
Unknown assessor identity or awareness does not prevent conditional reasoning about whether the measurement could be influenced if awareness existed.

considerations: Assess whether knowledge could influence this outcome. Evidence that influence actually occurred belongs to 4.5; its absence does not resolve 4.4.

Possible influence requires a judgement or reporting pathway through which assessor awareness could matter. Awareness alone is not a measurement difference, and a susceptible outcome does not by itself show that influence was possible in this assessment.
When a composite mixes objective and subjective components, assess each component's pathway separately and retain uncertainty where a component-specific link is unresolved.
questions.decision_rule: Knowledge could influence participant-reported outcomes, observer-reported outcomes involving judgement, and intervention-provider decisions; it is unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes without judgement, such as all-cause mortality. A standardized instrument does not remove judgment from elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment.

questions.bias_construct: Whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced outcome assessment. Require evidence or strong beliefs plus a judgement opportunity; awareness alone does not establish influence.
considerations: Possible influence without evidence it occurred maps differently from likely influence.

Likely influence requires more than assessor awareness or a possible pathway: look for evidence it occurred, or strong beliefs and a real judgement opportunity. Keep this conclusion separate from measurement susceptibility and detection opportunity.
Objective components can provide valid reassurance for those components without overriding likely influence or unresolved Evidence for subjective components in the same Result.
questions.decision_rule: Distinguish possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from likely influence. Strong beliefs about benefits or harms make influence more likely, for example patient-reported symptoms or recovery assessed by an intervention provider. A standardized scale or grading rule does not by itself remove an elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment pathway.

fidence intervals are at the 95% level. Prespeci-
fied subgroup analyses looked at the consistency
of treatment effect according to stratification
factors, time period, categorized Gleason score,
and quintiles of PSA levels that were measured
before the initiation of long-term ADT. Key sub-
group analyses according to metastatic status
were prespecified. Exploratory analyses considered
prostate cancer-specific survival and progression-
free survival according to the age at random-
ization.
All the patients were included in the efficacy
analyses under their assigned treatment on an
intention-to-treat basis. For safety analyses, pa-
tients were grouped according to the treatment
that they started. In the analysis of the median
duration of abiraterone treatment, data were cen-
sored at the date of last contact with the patient
if the patient had not reported stopping the drug.
Results
Patients
Between November 15, 2011, and January 17,
2014, a total of 1917 consenting patients at 111
U.K. and 5 Swiss sites underwent randomization
(957 to ADT alone and 960 to combination
therapy). Data were frozen on February 10, 2017.
The flow of patients through the trial is shown
in Figure S1 in the Supplementary Appendix,
available at NEJM.org; the baseline characteris-
tics of the patients are shown in Table 1, and in
Table S1 in the Supplementary Appendix. The
median PSA level was 53 ng per milliliter. The
median follow-up was 40 months.
Treatment
The median time from randomization to the ini-
tiation of abiraterone was 1.3 weeks, and the
median time from the initiation of ADT to the
initiation of abiraterone was 8.0 weeks (most pa-
tients started ADT before randomization) (Table
S2 in the Supplementary Appendix). Of the 960
patients in the combination group, 10 (1%) did
not receive abiraterone, mostly because they de-
clined treatment. The median duration of abira
terone treatment was 23.7 months in the patients
for whom the duration was capped at 2 years
(67% reported stopping for treatment comple-
tion) and 33.2 months in the patients who could
continue through progression (51% reported per-
manent stopping for progression and 20% for
excessive toxic effects) (Table S2 and Fig. S2 in
the Supplementary Appendix). A total of 265
patients (28%) had not yet permanently stopped
treatment with abiraterone at the time of this
report.
The planned rate of use of radiotherapy was
41% in the combination group and in the ADT-
alone group. The reported rate of use of radio-
therapy was 39% in the combination group and
40% in the ADT-alone group.
Overall Survival
There were 184 deaths in the combination group
and 262 in the ADT-alone group. There was
strong evidence of a survival advantage in the
combination group, with a 3-year survival of
83% as compared with 76% in the ADT-alone
group (hazard ratio for death, 0.63; 95% confi-
dence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.76; P<0.001) (Fig. 1A).

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data; a source creation date, registry posting or update date, amendment date, or retrieval date is not automatically the relevant trial chronology.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent, and a data cutoff is not investigator unblinding. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; pre-unblinding finalization differs from ambiguous chronology only in the timing premise.
